1) [Seif 1] One must blow the shofar while standing. Scripture states, "It shall be a day of teruah for you," and we derive the word "for you" from the same expression stated regarding the Omer and counting the Omer, which are performed standing, as it says, "From when the sickle begins upon the standing grain." Do not read it merely as "standing grain," but as "standing upright." Tur. Hagahot Maimoniyot, chapter 3, writes likewise in the name of Sefer Mitzvot Katan, and Beit Yosef cites it. Kesef Mishneh, Hilchot Temidin UMusafin, law 23, writes in the name of R' Yitzchak ibn Ghayyat that this was received as a tradition from our teachers and supported by the verse. This was cited above in siman 489, letter 15. Birkei Yosef, here letter 1, likewise cites it and writes that we find the same in Midrash Pesikta, Parashat Lech Lecha and Parashat Emor, as he wrote above in siman 8. In siman 8, letter 2, he cites Pesikta that we learn from the Omer regarding every mitzvah in which the word "for you" appears, such as brit milah, tzitzit, and lulav: "Every male among you shall undergo brit milah," "It shall be for you as tzitzit," and "You shall take for yourselves." All of these mitzvot are performed standing.

Accordingly, it appears that the blessing too should be recited standing, as with the Omer and tzitzit. Yad Ephraim on Magen Avraham, seif katan 1, writes likewise, as do Mateh Ephraim, letter 3; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 4; and Mishnah Berurah, letter 1. It also appears that one who hears the blessing from the shaliach tzibbur in order to fulfill his obligation should stand, because hearing is considered equivalent to responding. Machatzit HaShekel at the beginning of siman 690 writes likewise. Ben Ish Chai, Parashat Nitzavim, letter 15, however, writes that some places have the custom to stand during the blessing over shofar and some do not; in his city the custom was not to stand.

2) Know that the gezeirah shavah deriving "for you" regarding shofar from "for you" regarding the Omer applies also to the listeners. Since the principal shofar blasts are those of Mussaf, one need stand only for them, and they are therefore called the blasts sounded while standing. The earlier blasts, called the blasts sounded while seated, are primarily to confuse the Satan. The blower himself was required to stand because mitzvot of this type are performed standing, or alternatively because of the honor of the congregation. Radbaz, part 1, siman 25; Mor Uketziah; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 2; Mateh Yehudah; Machazik Berachah, letter 1; Erech HaShulchan, letter 1. Erech HaShulchan notes that manuscript rulings of R' Yeshayah the First hold that the blasts sounded while seated are the principal ones. In his Chukat HaPesach, however, in the addenda to this siman, he agrees with Radbaz. The later authorities rule likewise.

3) One who did not hear the shofar blasts in the order of the blessings and then comes to hear them must stand while listening. Radbaz; Magen Avraham, seif katan 1; Shulchan Gavoah, letter 3; Birkei Yosef, letter 3; Shaarei Teshuvah, letter 1. Likewise, an individual who hears the shofar in order to fulfill his obligation and will not later hear the blasts in the order of the blessings must stand. If he heard them while seated, he fulfilled his obligation. Mateh Ephraim, letter 5; Mishnah Berurah, letter 2. See below, letter 5.

4) "One must blow while standing." One should not lean upon something in such a way that if the support were removed he would fall. Derashot Maharil, Hilchot Shofar; Darkei Moshe; Magen Avraham; Pri Chadash; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 1; Birkei Yosef, letter 4; Shaarei Teshuvah; Shulchan Aruch HaRav, letter 1; Chayei Adam, rule 141, letter 6; Mateh Ephraim; Mishnah Berurah.

5) "One must blow while standing." If he blew while seated, he fulfilled his obligation, because shofar is derived from the Omer, and regarding the Omer itself one fulfills the obligation after the fact while seated, as stated in siman 489. Magen Avraham; Pri Chadash; Eliyah Rabbah, letter 3; Birkei Yosef, letter 2; Shulchan Aruch HaRav; Chayei Adam; Mateh Ephraim; Mishnah Berurah. See above, siman 489, letter 16. If the blower has already fulfilled his obligation and blows for another individual, he may blow while seated, but the listener must stand. Siddur Amudei Shamayim; Pithei Olam, letter 2.

"To fulfill," etc. Mahari Abuhav gives another reason: if we did not mention the attribute of night during the day, it would appear that darkness is evil, but this is not so, for "He made everything beautiful in its time." The Shulchan Aruch omitted this reason because Beit Yosef objected that according to it we should not need to mention the attribute of day at night. In my humble opinion there is no difficulty. Mahari Abuhav's intent is that whenever we bless over 1 matter alone, it can imply that its opposite is bad. Accordingly, if we failed to mention day at night, it could similarly appear that light is bad. This is easy to understand.

1) [Seif 1] "Blessed are You, Hashem our God, King of the universe, Who forms light," etc. The reason a blessing is recited every day over the light of the sun, unlike the blessing over fire, which is recited only on Motzaei Shabbos, is that sunlight is renewed each day. Tosafot writes likewise in Perek Makom Shenahagu. Pri Chadash, letter 1; Shalmei Tzibbur, page 90c.

2) There, "Who forms light," etc. When beginning this blessing, one should touch the arm tefillin, which correspond to Beriah in the aspect of action, corresponding to the prayer of Yotzer, which is in Beriah in the aspect of speech. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse on Yotzer and Kriat Shema, page 18d, and in the prayer text, page 51b. This was cited above in siman 48. See also what we wrote in siman 25, letters 27 and 32, and siman 48, letter 1, beginning "Know also this introduction."

When touching the arm tefillin during Yotzer Or, one should touch it when saying the word "u'vorei" in "u'vorei choshech," because that word alludes to Beriah, as stated in Shaar HaKavanos, page 19a. One should not touch the head tefillin now at the beginning of Yotzer Or. Rather, when he reaches Shemoneh Esrei he should touch the head tefillin, because both correspond to Atzilut: the head tefillin in the aspect of action and the prayer in the aspect of speech. This is explained in Shaar HaKavanos, the first and third discourses on the morning prayer and the first discourse on the Amidah.

I likewise saw written in the name of Rabbi Shmuel Vital, in manuscript on the margin of Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Kriat Shema, chapter 1, regarding the Arizal's statement that at the beginning of the ascent of Beriah, namely Yotzer Or, one should hold and touch the arm tefillin. It says: "This is correct, because Yotzer and the arm tefillin are both in Beriah, as explained by us. Therefore one should touch specifically the arm tefillin at Yotzer Or and not the head tefillin until the beginning of the Amidah. For this reason the Rav omitted touching the head tefillin at u'vorei choshech." End quote. Shalmei Tzibbur likewise writes in the name of the Rav that before beginning Yotzer Or one should touch the arm tefillin, and before beginning the Amidah one should touch the head tefillin.

Chesed LaAlafim similarly writes: "When saying Yotzer Or, one should touch the arm tefillin. One should not touch the head tefillin until immediately before the silent Shemoneh Esrei. This is the correct practice according to the mystical tradition and the custom of the community of pietists in the Beit El study hall in Jerusalem." Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi and Ben Ish Chai write likewise. This is contrary to Mishnat Chassidim, cited by Yad Aharon and Baer Heitev, which states that one touches the arm tefillin at Yotzer Or and the head tefillin at u'vorei choshech. Rather, one should not touch the head tefillin until Shemoneh Esrei. One should touch it after saying, "Hashem, open my lips," and before beginning the Amidah, for there begins the aspect of Atzilut, as explained in Shaar HaKavanos, first discourse on the Amidah, page 28d.

3) There, "Who forms light." The blessing Yotzer Or, Shemoneh Esrei, and Birkat HaMazon each contain every letter of the alphabet except the final form of the letter peh. This teaches that one who concentrates during these 3 is protected so that Satan, an evil occurrence, or any prosecutor, even when wrath surges, has no power over his prayer or his meal. Ateret Zekenim; Shalmei Tzibbur, page 90b.

4) There, "Who forms light." One must pause between Yotzer and Or so that the words do not sound like "Yotzeror." Ateret Zekenim; Shalmei Tzibbur. The later authorities write likewise. See what we wrote above in siman 48, letter 1, in the name of Shaar HaKavanos regarding points of precise pronunciation that pertain to this blessing.

5) "Alone, from then." When saying the word me'az, one should intend the union represented by the combined Divine Name Yahadonai, because the numerical value of az is 8, corresponding to the 8 letters of that Name. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse on the intentions of Yotzer, page 19a; Shalmei Tzibbur, page 90d; Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi, siman 14, letter 4.

2) There, "Who forms light," etc. When beginning this blessing, one should touch the arm tefillin, which correspond to Beriah in the aspect of action, parallel to the prayer of Yotzer, which is in Beriah in the aspect of speech. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse on Yotzer and Kriat Shema, page 18d, and in the prayer text, page 51b. This was cited above in siman 48. See also what we wrote above in siman 25, letters 27 and 32, and in siman 48, letter 1.

When touching the arm tefillin during Yotzer Or, one should do so when saying the word "u'vorei" in the phrase "u'vorei choshech," because it alludes to Beriah, as stated in Shaar HaKavanos, page 19a. One should not touch the head tefillin now at the beginning of Yotzer Or. Rather, when he reaches Shemoneh Esrei he should touch the head tefillin, because both correspond to Atzilut: the head tefillin in the aspect of action and the prayer in the aspect of speech. This is explained in Shaar HaKavanos, the first and third discourses on the morning prayer and the first discourse on the Amidah.

Rabbi Shmuel Vital likewise wrote in manuscript that because Yotzer and the arm tefillin both correspond to Beriah, one should specifically touch the arm tefillin during Yotzer Or and not the head tefillin until the beginning of the Amidah. Shalmei Tzibbur writes similarly in the name of the Rav: before beginning Yotzer Or one touches the arm tefillin, and before beginning the Amidah one touches the head tefillin.

Chesed LaAlafim writes: "When saying Yotzer Or, one should touch the arm tefillin. One should not touch the head tefillin until immediately before the silent Shemoneh Esrei. This is the correct mystical practice, and this is the practice of the community of pietists in the Beit El study hall in Jerusalem." Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi and Ben Ish Chai likewise rule this way. This is contrary to Mishnat Chassidim, cited by Yad Aharon and Baer Heitev, which states that at Yotzer Or one touches the arm tefillin and at u'vorei choshech one touches the head tefillin. Rather, one should not touch the head tefillin until Shemoneh Esrei, as stated above. One should touch it after saying, "Hashem, open my lips," and before beginning the prayer, because that is where the aspect of Atzilut begins.

3) There, "Who forms light." We find that Yotzer Or, Shemoneh Esrei, and Birkat HaMazon each contain every letter of the alphabet except the final form of peh. This teaches that one who concentrates during these 3 is protected so that Satan, an evil occurrence, and any prosecutor, even when wrath surges, has no power over his prayer or meal. Ateret Zekenim; Shalmei Tzibbur.

4) There, "Who forms light." One must pause between Yotzer and Or so that they do not sound as a single word. Ateret Zekenim; Shalmei Tzibbur. The later authorities write likewise.

5) "Alone, from then." When saying me'az, one should intend the union represented by the combined Divine Name Yahadonai, because the numerical value of az is 8, corresponding to the 8 letters of that Name. Shaar HaKavanos; Shalmei Tzibbur; Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi.
